1:
Chrysostom hears a deliberate lowering of the voice. Having said great things and set himself and all the faithful above Moses, the writer moderates his tone again, since the false apostles made it necessary both to lift his hearers and to bring the swelling down — though not to undo it, which would be a trifler's part. He manages it by making everything mercy rather than merit: nothing was contributed except that they became ministers and made themselves subservient to what God gave, which is why the word chosen was not largess nor supply but ministry. Calvin reaches the same conclusion by another road, that the writer premises he had not come to such a pinnacle by his own efforts, and notes that grounding the apostleship in God's mercy says more than grounding it in his grace. Ellicott finds two thoughts rising together at the word, his own unworthiness of the office and the trials in which it had to be discharged, and makes the calling itself the answer to both. Henry adds that the dignity did not breed idleness but diligence, and that the strength to persevere came from the same mercy that gave the office.

On the verb itself Robertson supplies the colour, that it means to behave badly under pressure and so to lose heart, and that the man it describes is the faint-hearted coward. Clarke reports a variant that turns the clause round altogether, some copies reading not we faint not but we act not wickedly, which one editor thought the true text and which joins smoothly to what follows. What follows is renounced, and Barnes takes the word at its root, to speak off or away from, a verb found nowhere else in these writings, and sets the renunciation against the religions of the nations, which were largely made up of trick and were kept up by deceiving the ignorant. His conclusion is a rule rather than a comment: truth never needs such arts, no cause long succeeds by cunning, and religion is open and straightforward, having no alliance with artifice. Gill puts the same thing as consistency, that they were the same men in public as in private, using no art to cover either doctrine or life.

What the hidden things of shame are is disputed three ways. Clarke passes on the opinion that carnal abominations are meant, and observes that there were people at Corinth who taught fornication to be no sin. Ellicott grants that the English word once carried that wider sense, but holds the context points not to sensual vice nor to dishonesty in the modern meaning but to subtlety and underhand dealing, and reconstructs the dilemma his opponents had built, that his change of plan showed either a discreditable fickleness or something worse. Calvin canvasses the readings and takes a third, that the phrase covers every disguise by which the gospel was adulterated; his image is of chaste women content with natural beauty and needing no artificial adorning, against harlots who never think themselves adorned enough until nature has been corrupted. Robertson traces the two remaining words to their roots, one meaning a doer of any deed whatever and so a clever man, the other coming from a word for bait and used of watering down gold or wine. Clarke brings that forward to his own day and names the practices — softening the unpopular part of a creed, affecting moderation to gather a larger audience, leaving the fashionable vices alone, calling dissipation relaxation — and Wesley sums the whole of it as accommodating the word to the taste of the hearers.
3:
The objection being met is obvious enough and Gill states it plainly: people sat under the preaching and saw no glory in it, which looks like an answer to everything claimed for the gospel's clearness. Barnes concedes the fact and refuses the inference, since the failure is not in the message, not a concealment God intended, and not a want of light in the thing itself. He hears a deliberate echo of the veil the lawgiver put on his own face, and turns it round: there is a veil here too, but it lies elsewhere. Ellicott makes the same move by correcting two tenses, so that the gospel has been veiled and the people concerned are perishing rather than lost, and he insists the present participle leaves the door open, since a man on that road may yet turn from it. He also widens the class, against those who confine it to Judaising teachers, to all who are at present on the way to perish. Calvin puts it hardest of the three, treating the failure to see as itself the evidence, and adding the image that settles it: the sun is not less resplendent because the blind do not perceive his light.

Who is meant by the god of this world is the chapter's sharpest question, and one of them breaks ranks. Calvin says no one judging rightly can doubt that Satan is meant. Gill agrees and explains the title carefully, since it is owed not to any hand in making or governing the world but to his hold over the worst and greatest part of it. Ellicott puts it as a consequence rather than an office, that a world worshipping hatred and falsehood and selfishness has in effect deified the devil. Robertson gives the word its narrower sense, the god of this age. Against all of them Clarke admits a considerable reluctance to give the title to Satan at all, and says that but for a rooted prejudice in favour of the common opinion the other view might be well vindicated, that the supreme God is meant, who in judgment gave the unbelieving over to darkness. Barnes reports that some of the Fathers held exactly this, and names Clarke as inclining to it, before setting it aside and explaining that the name god is given here not for any divine attribute but because this is the being the world actually serves.

Calvin then accounts for the older reading historically, and the account is unusually candid about his own side. Hilary, pressed by opponents who used the verse against the divinity of Christ, twisted it into a statement that God had blinded the understandings of this world; Chrysostom followed him in order to avoid conceding two principles to the Manicheans, and Augustine had the same reason, while what moved Ambrose does not appear. His verdict is on the method rather than the men: this is what the heat of controversy does, since being harassed by opponents they were more concerned to refute them than to find out what was actually meant. Cyril preserves a specimen of the very dispute, where the heretic asks what sort of God causes blindness and is answered from the preceding verse, that the veil lies on those who are perishing, with the further question whether the Lord did not himself speak in parables so that seeing they might not see — not from hatred but because they had closed their own eyes, so that where there is wilful wickedness grace is withheld. Robertson reaches the same point grammatically, that they refused to believe and so the blinding followed, which is what happens with wilful disbelievers; and Wesley calls the description of Satan here at once sublime and horrible.
5:
Ellicott hears an answer to a charge that he had been egotistic in his preaching, and reports the repudiation as indignant. Robertson agrees in a sentence, that a preacher could hardly find a poorer or more disgusting topic than himself. Gill spells out what preaching oneself would amount to: devising one's own doctrine, lording it over consciences, displaying learning, gathering wealth, or teaching that human nature is sound and salvation earned. Calvin reports a proposal to read the sentence as a compressed antithesis, we preach not ourselves to be lords but Christ to be the one Lord, and while not objecting he prefers the wider sense, since a man may preach himself otherwise than by claiming dominion — by aiming at display rather than edification, by wanting distinction, by making the work pay. Clarke takes the three titles in turn, the Anointed whom the prophets foretold, the Saviour who delivers from sins, and the Ruler who has all power, and glosses the last clause by saying they laboured as faithfully for eternal interests as a trusted slave does for his master's affairs.

Cyril turns the verse into evidence. This preacher was the former persecutor, and he asks what accounts for the change: not a bribe, since none was offered, and not the sight of Christ on earth, since by then he had been taken up. The witness of friends was weighty but open to suspicion, whereas of a man once the enemy who afterwards died for his sake, who can doubt? On the verse that follows, Ellicott sets it in direct opposition to what went before, the god of this world doing his work of blinding and the true God calling light out of darkness, and points out that the verb refers to one definite past moment rather than a continuing state. Clarke argues from the same parallel that the gospel is no human invention, the author of light being its author too. Robertson makes the image domestic, a lamp lit in the heart, where miners carry theirs on the forehead. Calvin canvasses four ways of taking the clause, rejects two as subtleties that do not answer to the writer's intention, and settles on the reading that alludes to the creation, since the passage from visible light to spiritual has elegance and nothing forced about it. Barnes adds that what was lit in them came neither from human reasoning nor from tradition but directly from the source of all light, and Wesley marks the comparison implied, since this face reflects the glory in another manner than the face of Moses did.

The treasure and its container are handled by all of them. Gill explains why the gospel deserves the name, for the worth of its truths, the blessings it carries and the promises it holds out. Ellicott supplies the custom behind the image, that eastern kings kept their gold in earthenware jars, and hears a side glance at the taunts about the apostle's bodily weakness — let it be granted, he says, and let it show whose the power is. Calvin makes that reversal the whole point, since treasure is commonly laid up not in a splendid chest but in a mean one, so the thing most damaging to his standing is turned into an argument for it. Clarke works on the word, which he says means a vessel of shell, brittle as the shell that is a fish's outer part, and recalls the philosophers who gave a man two bodies and called one the chariot of the soul; he adds the distinction between clay that has been through the kiln and clay that has not, the fired vessel being past mending once broken. Robertson keeps to the same root, baked clay, the material of the inscribed fragments turned up in Egypt, and states the purpose bluntly: God, not man, is the dynamo.
8:
Where the four antitheses get their colour from is disputed. Clarke refers them wholesale to the Isthmian games, dividing them three to wrestling and one to the footrace, and glosses each by the technical usage — the gripe an opponent cannot break, the runner pressed hard from behind but never overtaken, the fall that does not end the bout. Ellicott hears a soldier instead, hemmed in but with room to move, pursued but not abandoned, struck down as by a javelin but not perishing, and compares the faint yet pursuing of the old narrative. Barnes leaves the choice open between wrestlers and gladiators. Robertson takes the first verb back to the pressing of grapes and catches the play in the last pair, lost but not lost out. Chrysostom reads the whole series as a demonstration rather than a complaint: it is marvellous enough that the treasure is kept in such a vessel, but more so that it survives ten thousand hardships, since a vessel of adamant would have been neither strong enough to carry so vast a treasure nor proof against so many machinations. He notices the method too, that contraries are set side by side on purpose to show whose the strength is.

Whether the pressure is inward or outward divides two of them exactly. Wesley assigns the first four terms to inward affliction and the next four to outward, and reads each clause as showing the earthen vessel in its first half and the power in its second. Calvin insists the trouble is external and argues it from the word, which he says means a thing dashed against from outside, like waves breaking on a rock that make a great noise round about it and no commotion in it; and of the second term he says it describes a compression so close that a man cannot draw breath, so that the denial means they could breathe well enough for all that. Henry keeps to the sense rather than the etymology, that they were not hedged in or cooped up because they could see help in God and had liberty of access to him, and that good men may be forsaken by their friends but not by him. Gill widens the first phrase three ways at once, taking it of every place, of every hour, and of every sort of person, since even weak believers among the children of God gave them trouble.

On what the dying of Jesus means Ellicott stands alone against the rest. He makes the word mean deadness, the state of a corpse, and reads it of a life spent in one long conflict with illness, so that the writer dragged about with him what it was hardly an exaggeration to call a living corpse; and at the next verse he says outright that the usual reading, which refers the words to the dangers of persecution, is in his judgment wrong, since the tenor of the letter points instead to a daily struggle with pain and weakness. Everyone else takes it the other way. Barnes sees the marks of violence on the body and an expectation of dying as his Master died; Clarke sees the wounds and bruises that contenders carried through life; Robertson wonders whether the stoning at Lystra is in view; Wesley reads it as the continual expectation of laying life down. The closing antithesis divides them again. Calvin takes it as irony, since it was unseemly that the Corinthians should be at their ease while he struggled, and they had contrived a Christianity without a cross and then despised the servants of Christ for not being as comfortable as themselves. Ellicott hears the pathos of the earlier letter but says the irony is precisely what is absent here.
13:
Whether the spirit of faith is the Holy Spirit divides them at once. Gill says it is, since the faith in question is not of our own power but the free gift and operation of God, which is why the Spirit is named from it. Barnes denies the identification and makes the phrase mean substantially the same as faith itself, a believing sense of the truth. Ellicott takes a middle position, neither the Divine Spirit outright nor merely a temper of mind, but the human spirit in fellowship with the Divine and so marked by faith. Whose faith is called the same divides them again. Wesley refers it to the saints of old and to David in particular. Calvin knows that reading, grants it is true in itself, and rejects it as not answering to the argument, since it is not Abraham or the fathers that the writer is joining himself to here but the Corinthians — the point being that a difference in how gently God deals with each is no bar to one inheritance, because where there is oneness of faith there will be oneness of hope. Robertson draws a chronological inference from the next clause, that its wording shows the writer was not certain of being alive when Christ returns, against what has been concluded from three passages in the earlier letter.

On the resurrection itself they close ranks. Barnes makes the assurance the thing that carried them through persecution, since they knew their trials would soon end. Clarke says they do not fear even sealing the truth with their blood, being persuaded their bodies will be raised as their Master's was. Gill distributes the agency carefully, referring the raising chiefly to the Father while denying that the Son and Spirit were uninvolved, and refusing to make Christ a mere instrument in the raising of the saints. Henry states the practical use, that faith is an effectual remedy against fainting and sets a man above the fear of death. Ellicott adds a textual note and a caution: the better copies read that we shall be raised with Jesus rather than by him, the other reading having apparently arisen from a wish to fit the words to the fact that Christ was already risen; and he insists that what is promised here is not any deliverance from danger or illness but the resurrection itself.

The last verse is read as an argument for sympathy. Calvin makes it the point at which the writer stops distinguishing himself from them: if he is afflicted it is on their account, so they had good reason to take a share of it on themselves, and the consolation offered is that while God spares the weak and deals with them gently, those of more distinguished strength are afflicted for the common advantage of all — from which it follows that the Corinthians, unable to help him otherwise, should at least help by their prayers and their fellow-feeling. Barnes suspects a nearer motive as well, that stating this would conciliate the faction at Corinth that had turned against him. On the closing clause Ellicott finds the construction genuinely obscure, offers as the best sense that grace, having abounded through the greater part of them, may make thanksgiving overflow to God's glory, lists two further renderings the Greek will bear, and observes that the English version is not one of them. Clarke reads the same clause as a wish that the gratitude of the converted may keep pace with the blessings they have received; Robertson catches the play by which more is made through the more; and Wesley puts the mechanism in five words, that thanksgiving invites more abundant grace.
16:
Barnes reads the pair of terms as an anthropology and says so: the writer describes two parts so distinct that one decays while the other is renewed, and by using them he shows he was no materialist. Robertson keeps the same contrast but puts it as process, the decay of the bodily organism set against a growth in grace, and notes that the phrase for day by day occurs nowhere else in these writings and may be a colloquial repetition. Clarke reports a rabbinic opinion that even spirits need continual renovation, God renewing the angels daily by returning them to the fiery river they came from. He also returns to the textual variant he had raised at the chapter's opening, observing that the same two readings stand here, that the editor who preferred the rarer one at the first verse follows the common one here, and that the common reading suits the sense better. Calvin hears the tone lift, as of a man who has carried his point, and turns it against his readers, since they had been valuing a teacher the further he stood from the cross.

The sentence that follows draws admiration from all of them and two try to say why. Clarke passes on a judgment that the passage is among the most emphatic in these letters and that its author speaks here as much like an orator as an apostle, that the lightness claimed is levity itself by comparison, and that the doubled phrase cannot be rendered at all, since one may pass from hyperbole to hyperbole and still fall infinitely below what is meant; he adds the observation that the Hebrew word for heavy also means glorious, so that weight and glory are joined here by an ear trained in that language. Barnes reports a comparison with Demosthenes and says the writer's mind was labouring to convey what language could only imperfectly carry — while noting that to most people the trials listed would have seemed anything but light. Ellicott prefers the present lightness of our affliction as both more literal and better balanced, and explains the doubled phrase as the Hebrew way of marking intensity by repetition. Robertson calls it piling one mountain on another and sets out the four contrasted pairs. Wesley says only that the beauty of it can be preserved in no translation or paraphrase, every one of which must sink infinitely below the original.

The last verse is taken as a condition rather than a description. Clarke renders the participle as aiming rather than looking and then states the limit plainly: the affliction works this weight of glory only for those who are not looking at what is seen, since a man may be grievously afflicted with his eye still bent on temporal good and derive no benefit at all from it. Barnes says the same thing positively, that here is the true secret of bearing trials with patience, and that suffering contemplated by itself grows heavy and long while suffering set beside eternal blessedness becomes bearable. Ellicott glosses the verb as the contemplation of a goal one is striving towards, and sets beside it a sentence from a contemporary moralist, that the things most men seek are objects of imagination which make a show of being for a time, so that the mind should be given to what is eternal. Calvin makes the measure the thing that changes: a moment is long while we look about us on this side and that, but once the mind is raised heavenward a thousand years begin to look like a moment. Gill offers a second sense for the things that are seen, that they may be the afflictions themselves, which are equally open to the senses and equally temporary, so that a believer is not to stand poring over his own troubles.
